#787. Beverly Hills, 90210 Alum Kimmarie Johnson’s Cause of Death Revealed

Kimmarie Johnson, who appeared on Beverly Hills, 90210 in 1998, died as a result of cardiopulmonary arrest, with ovarian cancer as an underlying cause, per her death certificate.

Authorities have determined what led to Kimmarie Johnson’s death.

Two weeks after the actress, who appeared in Beverly Hills, 90210 and Dude, Where’s My Car?, died Nov. 3 following what her niece described as a “heart event,” her cause of death was determined to be cardiopulmonary arrest, according to a death certificate obtained by People, who listed her age as 59.

While a heart attack—medically referred to as myocardial infarction—is the result of a blocked artery, cardiopulmonary arrest—or cardiac arrest—is when the heart stops beating and is unable to effectively pump blood to the body, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Johnson’s death certificate also listed an underlying cause as metastatic granulosa cell ovarian tumor with peritoneal carcinomatosis, meaning the rare type of ovarian cancer she had spread to her abdominal area, according to the Mayo Clinic.

After her death, Johnson’s niece Rhonda Scott reflected on the joy her aunt brought into the world.

“She radiated a light so strong and bright,” Scott told People in an interview published Nov. 5. “People who came in contact with her felt nothing but positive energy. We will miss her tremendously and will continue to honor her life forever.”

Johnson graduated from Wilkinsburg High School in Pittsburgh in 1985 before studying at California University in Pennsylvania. She won the title of Miss Pennsylvania USA in 1993 and was subsequently a finalist at the Miss USA pageant.

She later moved to New York City and then Los Angeles, where she pursued a career in modeling. While Johnson found small roles on the big screen over the years, she launched her skincare brand SkinGlow by Kimmarie in 2011 and continued to model until her death.

She is survived by her son Cameron Nino, with whom she shared a special connection.

“My [son], u are bright, honest, kind, intelligent, funny and compassionate,” Johnson wrote on Facebook last November alongside a picture of her son for his 22nd birthday. “I’m glad that you enjoyed a good day.”

#786. Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury

England forward injured in Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne

Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’

Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted and the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, said that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

“I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany said after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

#785. Nicole Richie Reveals Daughter Kate Has “Surpassed” Her in This Way

Nicole Richie shared that when it comes to the world of beauty, her and husband Joel Madden's 18-year-old daughter Harlow Kate Madden has completely eclipsed her mom.

Nicole Richie has a simple solution for her beauty needs.

The Simple Life alum revealed that her and husband Joel Madden’s 18-year-old daughter Harlow Kate Madden has become her go-to makeup artist, as the teen is even more skilled than she is in that particular area.

“I would say that she has surpassed me,” Richie told People in an interview published Nov. 19. “She’s so good. I actually am not very good at doing my own makeup. She is a whole different animal.”

And the 45-year-old knows exactly how her daughter—who chooses to go by her middle name Kate—got so good at glowing up her family.

“She grew up watching YouTube tutorials,” Richie explained, “and she’s so well-versed in makeup and contour and highlighting and just all the things.”

“If I ever need my makeup done at home, I’m going to her,” the House of Harlow founder added. “It’s not me doing it ... She kills a cat-eye.”

Of course, Kate will soon be showing off more of her talents as she officially builds the foundation for a modeling career after signing with The Lions Management.

“I’ve always dreamed of modeling, so getting to start this next chapter with The Lions is incredibly exciting,” Kate shared in a Nov. 20 statement to Women’s Wear Daily. “Fashion has always been a way for me to express myself, and I can’t wait to explore that in a whole new way.”

She added, “I’m looking forward to learning, growing, meeting new people, and seeing where this journey takes me.”

Kate made her modeling debut alongside her mom for Balenciaga’s recent campaign celebrating the 25th anniversary of their Le City handbag, a style Richie was particularly fond of in the early 2000s.

And Madden—who also shares son Sparrow James Midnight, 17, with Richie—was particularly thrilled to see his daughter achieving her dream.

The Good Charlotte frontman reposted Kate’s modeling announcement to his Instagram Stories Nov. 20, captioning it with three red heart emojis and writing in all caps, “KATE!”

#783. Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?

A combination of smart analytics, a young manager and players hand-picked for their particular skills has the Seagulls flying high

They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.

But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.

It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.

If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.

According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.

They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.

The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?

On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.

“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”

Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.

Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”

When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.

When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.

Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”

One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.

Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear about how it informs your decision-making process, then it’s just a lot of data that doesn’t move the dial.”

The power of data is that it strips away emotions and preconceptions. When watching games, Hürzeler said he often identifies a player he thinks is performing well and texts Cave, only to learn that the numbers don’t support his impression. The conversation ends. “The numbers have to be right otherwise we have no chance of getting a player in.”

Conversely, the data identifies players he might not otherwise have considered – such as Diego Gómez, the Paraguayan signed from Inter Miami in 2024. Despite the strength of Gómez’s underlying numbers, the club had a free run at signing him. Cave suggested this reflected a misconception that players in MLS aren’t equipped to play in the Premier League. “What the data has allowed us to do is step away from some of those biases and just be clear on what the evidence tells us, to look at the signal rather than the noise.”

But identifying a player who can perform for Brighton is different from identifying one who will, Cave said. The club’s requirements are so specific that the data typically identifies only around five candidates, Hürzeler says, and fewer still are affordable. Of those remaining, the recruitment team and Hürzeler will speak to anyone with experience of them – players, coaches and sponsors – to learn more about their character and personality, and prepare dossiers. Together, they’ll identify a primary target and make a move. “It’s not like I get a list and then decide which players; it’s something we all decide together,” said Hürzeler.

As Barber explained: “The more we can find out about a player’s character the less risk there is of that player being rejected like a bad organ transplant.” There’s no exhaustive list of desirable characteristics, he added, but “coachability” is key. Brighton’s model hinges on players having the capacity to improve, and the best indication is their drive to do so. “The biggest element of coachability is attitude.”

Hürzeler asks himself: “What are they willing to give for their development? Are they willing to suffer?” He’s convinced this desire is innate. “These are things I can’t control.”

Conversations with people around Gómez painted a picture of “a boy that is clearly trying to get absolutely everything out of his career”, said Cave. But sometimes the qualities Brighton are looking for aren’t so obvious. Whereas the data is objective, says Barber, references are “someone’s opinion”. It’s challenging to know how much weight to give a single person’s negative judgment, particularly when it conflicts with other opinions, without dismissing it altogether. “Sometimes when you want to sign somebody you can subjectively screen out the negativity because you want them, and the data says you need them.”

Beyond character, the team consider a player’s ability to settle into a new country, and whether their partner will, too. Once Brighton make an offer, the player is normally keen to join, in Barber’s experience, because they know it can lead to a move to “potentially bigger things”. The selling club is often receptive because there are rarely any other comparable offers on the table.

But this has been changing, says Barber. Brighton’s success means their interest in a player “alerts other clubs to that talent”, creating competition. Selling clubs, meanwhile, have reason to believe that the player “has the potential to be valued for a lot more”. Increasingly, then, Brighton are having to pay more, making “our ability to trade profitably ever harder”.

Even if a deal can be agreed, it doesn’t always represent good business. As Cave explained: “You’re dealing with human beings, in a complex system and a complex game, so you will never have a 100% strike record.”

Asked what Brighton looks for in recruits, Gordon Greer, who played for the club from 2010 to 2016, was quick to answer: “high potential”. But that potential rarely means they’re ready to slot into the first‑team. Today, as Brighton’s pathway development manager, Greer’s job is to bridge that gap.

To understand how Greer does this, I joined him for coffee at the Lowry. He told me that he begins planning a player’s development while the club are still negotiating his signing. “In the buildup to us signing him, we’ll start to analyse him … what’s his strengths, what’s his weaknesses … where do we think we can help?” Once he’s met the player and understood their ambitions, he turns that assessment into a development plan.

To begin, Greer explained, he asked himself: “What are this player’s limiting factors to play for Brighton?” Sometimes the answer lies off the pitch. Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. It helps embed his playing principles by allowing the players to transmit them to each other. “We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch,” he explained. Other times the shortcomings are more directly related to football, such as back‑post defending. A typical one is physicality; Hürzeler’s counter-pressing requires repeated sprints and many recruits would risk injury if they were thrown into the first team. “The game is so fast, and the intensity is crazy,” Jack Hinshelwood, who made his first‑team debut in 2023, has said.

One pathway for development is the under-21s team, Greer says, but the physical demands of the game fall short of those in the Premier League. Hinshelwood, who came through the under-21s, suffered a stress fracture in his foot after a few top-flight games. “You need time to adapt,” he said. In Greer’s view, the level doesn’t challenge most recruits enough for them to learn. “We want to put them in a position where they’re stretched enough that they’re uncomfortable but they’ve got enough success that they’re doing things that they enjoy.”

An alternative is the loan market. Since 2018–19, Brighton have agreed more than 20 loan deals in each campaign. Playing time is an important consideration when arranging a loan, Greer explains, because a player’s value can drop if they’re not playing often. But he also considers the location, manager, formation and quality of the pitch. Position is crucial, too. Sending a striker to a team near the bottom of their league, where they’re likely to be living off scraps, can see their confidence and value drop, but sending a defender into the same environment can accelerate their development with repeated defensive situations. “You’re trying to get to a point where they’re impacting the game.”

A successful loan addresses a player’s limitations. “You’re trying to expose someone to something totally different,” Greer added. In 2017, Ben White – now of Arsenal and England – was loaned to Newport County to improve the “urgency in his defending”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The game model was end‑to-end, back-to-front, League Two, where you’re up against it,” Greer added. In 2024, Ibrahim Osman, shortly after signing from Nordsjælland in Denmark, went to Feyenoord, a possession-based team, to develop his technical game. “Physically, he was a beast, but he was quite untidy,” said Greer.

Throughout a loan, each player is continually reassessed. Those ready are brought into Hürzeler’s first team. If they’re not, another spell elsewhere might be arranged. But if their development has stalled for too long, they’ll be encouraged to leave permanently. That was the case with Leo Østigård, a Norway international signed from Molde in 2018. He was a skilled defender but he “wasn’t good enough on the ball”, Greer said. His development slowed down during a loan at Coventry, and then, at Stoke, it became “clear he wasn’t going to be for us”.

Rather than continuing to work on Østigård’s weaknesses, the club sought to maximise his strengths. A loan was arranged at Genoa, a defensive team where Østigård would shine. A year later, he signed for Napoli. “We tried everything but it didn’t work,” Greer said, “so we thought: ‘How do we create as much value as possible?’”

After speaking to Barber, I headed to Brighton’s training base, a short drive away from the Amex, to meet Hürzeler. Academy players milled around outside, while the first team was elsewhere preparing to face Getafe in the Conference League, a competition Brighton are being tipped to win.

I noticed a mural bearing the words: “Challenge the Establishment,” a reference to the so-called big six clubs. A member of staff pointed out that the mural had been Hürzeler’s idea, but the philosophy it exhibits has existed since Bloom took over the club in 2009. Brighton, the member of staff whispered to me, saw themselves as the “antidote” to big-spending clubs such as City.

Before Hürzeler and I sat down in the press conference room, another journalist asked him whether he thought Brighton could win the title. He dismissed the question. His focus was improving the team, he said. He suggested to me, however, that victories such as that over City were the fruits of his work developing the squad and an environment that allows talents to excel. “If you work with players for a longer time, you get used to each other and they get more and more of your principles.”

Hürzeler tells me he relies on older players who embody these principles, such as Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross. At 33, Hürzeler is younger than both, and became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in 2024. When you’re developing raw talents from abroad, while constantly selling and bringing in new players, you need a core group to “build the right culture”. Hinshelwood told me he has experienced this first-hand: “I remember watching their habits every day, how they live their lives, how they’re training, what they’re doing in the gym, how they’re communicating, and I learned so much just by watching them.”

Hürzeler also emphasised the importance of tailoring the support players receive. “You can’t treat a player like Yankuba Minteh who is coming from [the] Gambia the same as a player like Lewis Dunk, who comes from England,” he said. He wants to cultivate an environment in which, as he put it, players, “no matter which age, no matter from where they are coming from, can express themselves”.

To that end, Hürzeler appointed Mike Anthony, who spent 14 years working with New Zealand Rugby, as head of player development and high performance – a new role. One of Anthony’s priorities, he said, has been giving the players more responsibility. Players and the coaches increasingly “lead the programme together”, with players invited to lead discussions.

“They don’t want to just execute things, they want to be valued, they want to be appreciated, they want to be heard by us coaches,” Hürzeler said. “If you don’t give them ownership and responsibility off the pitch, how can you expect them to take responsibility for their own execution on the pitch? It’s not possible.”

A key part of his role, Hürzeler told me, is listening to his players. It helps them perform, and makes him a better coach. He was reminded of this in February 2025, when there were calls for him to lose his job after a poor run that included a 7-0 defeat at Nottingham Forest. James Milner and Danny Welbeck suggested he was overcomplicating his messaging around counter-pressing. Taking their advice on board, he made changes that helped turn things around. “It was definitely one reason why we turned around the results.”

Asked why Brighton have such a strong record for developing talent, Hinshelwood smiled: “You’re allowed to make mistakes, not effort mistakes, or applying yourself badly, but if you make a technical mistake you know you’ve got 10 other players who want you to try things,” he said.

Hürzeler also credited the club’s summer recruitment with this season’s success. Yet Brighton had sold Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham and Baleba to United, I pointed out. How could a club expect to improve while selling their best players?

Although he often tries to prevent departures by convincing Bloom not to sell, Hürzeler said he has no final say. “I can’t control whether a player gets a big offer and Tony wants to accept this offer.” But he’s come to see departures as an opportunity to revitalise the squad with new profiles. “When you sign for Brighton, you know that it’s part of the identity, so automatically you have the mindset that you have to deal with these things.”

Being transparent about the club’s model with coaches is a crucial component in their success, according to Barber, but even then it can create tensions. The decision to sell Caicedo was one reason De Zerbi departed, as was the Italian’s insistence on big-name signings rather than trusting the data. It’s no different with supporters, Barber said: “Sometimes when a big player leaves a club and the fans are blindsided by that, it creates this bigger sense of injustice, anger, disappointment.”

Barber also explains that he must go to great lengths to keep costs down. “The difference between what we bring in and what we spend is what we put out on the pitch.” The club’s use of experienced players such as Dunk is ultimately driven by financial constraints. They can’t afford to sign players in their prime, either in transfer fees or wages, so rely on players a little past their prime to counterbalance the inexperience of their younger recruits. “They’re providing that level of experience of a 27-, 28-, 29-year-old, albeit four or five years later, but at a much lower cost.”

Brighton also use data to identify and recruit coaches whose philosophy aligns with the existing squad, minimising the need to overhaul the squad to fit a new style of football. Hürzeler was identified in large part because the numbers showed he could build on the players he inherited. “Revolutions cost a lot of money,” Barber said. “If you can match the coach that you’re bringing into the squad that you’ve got, the cost of change is minimal.”

The final part of the model is knowing when to sell. Barber tries to have a replacement through the door before letting a player go. It becomes trickier to negotiate a fee for a replacement when the selling club knows Brighton have just sold a player for £100m. Barber told me he delayed selling Caicedo until he was confident Baleba could step up. “We felt Carlos had a lot of potential that we could help to realise quite quickly … he’s a quick learner and quite raw, but at the same time you could see rapid improvements in him.”

But other factors matter too, such as whether a player still has room to develop, and therefore increase his value further; the state of the market; and the risk that turning down an offer might jeopardise the chance of a future sale. “If there is a dearth of central midfielders at the moment, maybe now is the time to sell because there will be a significant premium because there are no other options.”

Barber adds that refusing to sell Caicedo to Arsenal in January 2023 was easier because other clubs wanted him in the summer. “Not doing the deal didn’t affect our ability to do the deal with Liverpool and then Chelsea the following summer.”

In their last match before the November international break, Brighton beat Brentford and leapfrogged City. They’d progressed in Europe too: a goal from Malick Yalcouyé, a £6m signing from ​​IFK Göteborg, had beaten Getafe. Outside the ground, fans were dreaming of titles. Barber said he hoped they would not have to wait much longer. “We now need to take the next step and put some silverware on the table.”

But if Brighton are to compete for major trophies, I wondered, will they have to invest more heavily in players, and keep them in their prime? Can the club’s current model allow them to become part of the establishment, rather than simply challenging it?

The club are already adapting, says Barber. The signing of Vuskovic for a club record £46m demonstrates an appetite for talents better equipped to immediately contribute to the first team. “Those players are already at a level of transfer fee that we wouldn’t have contemplated, and 10 years ago we wouldn’t have even considered.” As Jamestown’s algorithm improves, Barber says, he’s hopeful it will become easier for the club to invest these sorts of sums in players, because the risk of getting the assessment wrong will be lower.

But Barber believes player trading is likely to stay as the core of the club’s strategy, partly because they are good at it, but also because they need the revenue. “There’s always going to be this gap [in commercial sales and ticket revenue] so the need for us to trade will always be there.” Even if they did decide to keep players such as Baleba and Van Hecke, would they be able to? As much as a title or two might make it easier to convince top players to stay, Barber said he struggles to envisage a time when they’ll be able to compete with the bigger clubs on wages.

And even if Brighton could one day afford to retain their best players, would it make them less attractive to the next generation of recruits, who might no longer see the club as a stepping stone on the way to the so-called establishment? Could the club become so successful that the prices of their targets rise beyond what they can afford? Might the model self-cannibalise?

Hürzeler tells me he reflects on these same questions. “It’s interesting, this discussion, because these kinds of discussions we also have in the building.” When we spoke on the phone before the Hull match, I brought up Hearts, who have partnered with Jamestown and came close to winning the Scottish title in May for the first time since 1960, challenging the Celtic-Rangers duopoly. I asked whether this gave him the belief that Brighton could go one step further and break the big clubs’ stranglehold.

“Of course, you see this as motivation for what is possible,” he said. He revealed a belief that he can lift a trophy with Brighton, which is why he has extended his contract to 2029. “When I see the team now, they are so into it, they are so committed to it.” He just wouldn’t say when. “Will it be this season? I don’t know. Will it be next season? I don’t know.” Beyond that, he tries not to give it much attention. “These kinds of questions, we can answer them one day.”

#782. Germany news: Police raid chapters of Gremium MC biker gang

Police in southwestern Germany launched major early-morning operations against a biker gang. The state of Baden-Württemberg is outlawing three of its chapters. Meanwhile, unions are planning more strikes.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news from or pertaining to Germany on November 12, 2026:

Luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz is halting investment at its facilities in Germany, a board members announced on Thursday.

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.

Germany's major IG Metall trade union has enabled the possibility of longer warning strikes amid difficult negotiations for industrial employees.

"The board of IG Metall has pave the way for 24-hour warning strikes in the metalworking and electrical industry," the union said on Thursday.

The union accuses employers of intransigence after three rounds of negotiations without clear progress.

On Wednesday, regional chapters appealed for authorization for full-day warning strikes — the last step before a full union vote and an indefinite labor dispute.

"This escalation is completely excessive and counterproductive," Udo Dinglreiter, the president of the employers' umbrella organization, Gesamtmetall, said. He said that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk.

IG Metall's first chairperson Christiane Benner countered that "the employers want to turn this round of collective bargaining into a dispute over principles." Another union official said they were offering what amounted to a real-terms pay cut rather than seeking solutions.

IG Metall is calling for a 5% pay increase and other improved conditions for some 3.7 million workers starting in November, while employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 coupled with a 1.3% increase starting in the summer of 2028.

The union estimates that around 464,000 employees took part in the initial wave of warning strikes that were limited to periods of hours, rather than full days.

Employers argue that they're treading a difficult line between trying not to cut jobs and meeting calls for improved pay amid widespread industrial sector layoffs in Germany in recent years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Tis the season, already. Preparations are underway around Germany and in several cities, Christmas markets are opening to the public.

Some markets are already open in Essen and in Hamburg, Duisburg's opens on Thursday, and Cologne's follows a day later.

The coupons.de website has sought to track the planned prices for mulled wine or Glühwein as the markets open their doors nationwide.

The bad news? These prices are rising like so many others. The better news? The year-on-year increase is actually smaller than overall inflation figures, at around 1%.

On average, a cup is liable to set you back around €4.60 (roughly $5.10). Not entirely surprisingly, Munich tops the nationwide pricing chart, with the price peaking at €7. Other sites nationwide tend not to have the gall even to charge 6 euros.

Bargain hunters determined to get the best value mulled wine will need to venture deep into the center of Germany — hardly its core tourist hub — to find the lowest prices starting at around €3.50.

Deposits for the cup, the "Pfand," are also only going in one direction, and in the meantime range from €1 all the way up to €5. But there's a strong argument, particularly with the better designs or after a memorable trip, that this can be money well spent as a memento!

Police in the Emsland region in the northwest near the border to the Netherlands have reported a major fire in a complex of residential and commercial buildings in Papenburg.

The fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon, police said the following morning, causing damages worth "at least €10 million ($11 million)." Several hundred emergency services personnel were deployed.

"Based on current findings, the fire broke out in the sauna area of a gym facility on site, and quickly spread to further parts of the complex of buildings," police wrote.

Two men were in the sauna at the time and initially tried to douse the flames but without success.

Police said the buildings were evacuated as the fire spread, with some surrounding buildings also being cleared as a precaution because of possible smoke-related dangers.

Several people were injured, police said, including the two men in the sauna area suffering mild burns and suspected smoke inhalation sickness. They were treated in a nearby hospital but soon discharged.

"There were also injuries among the first responders," police wrote. "Four police officers, two firefighters and members of the rescue teams suffered mild injuries, particularly via smoke inhalation."

The fire was only extinguished late on Wednesday night, several hours after it started. The area is sealed off, with possible risks of damaged buildings collapsing. Police have also launched investigations into the fire's cause, but said that at present, the area was not safe for that work to start at full scale.

Germany's largest credit bureau Creditreform has published its "2026 Debtors' Atlas."

It finds that 10.16% of German adults, or 7.36 million people, exhibit at least the early warning signs of excessive debt. A year ago the ratio was 9.74%.

"The financial situation of private consumers has further deteriorated," Patrik-Ludwig Hantzsch, Creditreform's head of economic research, said. "In particular, the sharply increased living costs, energy costs and housing costs are straining expenditures."

Hantzsch said employment was also becoming an issue once more, saying "above all, well-paid jobs in manufacturing industries have been cut back in large numbers in recent months."

The report also highlights rising cases of signs of excessive debt prior to legal action being taken, such as payment reminders or warnings being sent, saying "consumers are taking on more credit-financed expenditures — increasingly also for smaller purchases — at simultaneously rising interest rates."

A larger share of men than women have excessive debts, perpetuating a longstanding trend.

People around the middle of their working lives, aged 30-39 and 40-49, are most likely to be affected — but the cohort with the fastest-rising share of people with excessive debts are young adults below the age of 30.

Bremen, Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt and North Rhine-Westphalia were among the states with the highest rates of excess debts, while the wealthy and fiscally conservative states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg had the lowest levels.

Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared the 27,000-point mark for the first time in its history in morning trading.

It climbed by around 1.3% in order to pass the milestone.

A combination of some positive outlook data from major companies, not least engineering giant Siemens, and the falling oil prices of recent days have helped fuel the uptick.

Siemens' shares had risen by almost 5%, to just over €291 (around $323) each, helping to spur on the gains and making the company the morning's top performer.

Despite several years of low growth and recession in the German economy, the DAX, like many Western indices, is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

Hundreds of police officers searched apartments and meeting sites for the biker group "Gremium MC" in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg early on Thursday.

The state interior ministry said the operation was part of a move to outlaw three sub-chapters of the group, the ones based in Böblingen and Leonberg, as well as the "Gremium MC Chapter Nomads Bosphorus Türkiye."

This last group was highlighted as a meaningful part of Gremium MC by security officials. It describes itself on Facebook as a great example that "people of different cultures and faiths can be strong together," featuring images of men posing with knives and other weapons.

Gremium MC prominently incorporates into its iconography the symbol of the Prussian military medal for exceptional valor, the Iron Cross, which was discontinued after World War I, reintroduced by Adolf Hitler during World War II, and then scrapped for good.

State Interior Minister Manuel Hagel was expected to make further comments later in the day in Ludwigsburg.

Gremium MC is deemed an "outlaw motorcycle gang" in Baden-Württemberg's latest security report, a term used for biker groups that do not recognize the state monopoly on the use of force and are often tied to organized crime.

"Extortion, drug dealing and pimping in particular tend to be part of their activities," state authorities say.

Baden-Württemberg counts 154 biker chapters in the state with around 2,000 members.

Founded in 1972 in Mannheim, various chapters of Gremium MC across the country have faced legal issues in recent years. In 2021, another chapter in the southwest, Gremium MC Southgate in Heidelberg, was outlawed on suspicion of organized crime activity.

Police in Hanover reported early on Thursday that three men were injured by an unknown driver in a car in the nearby town of Ronneberg.

One person sustained severe injuries in the incident late on Wednesday, police said.

Two of the wounded were taken to a nearby hospital while the other could be cared for at the scene.

Police said the driver fled the scene and that a search operation was ongoing. Authorities were also still investigating a potential motive for the apparent attack.

Today's updates start with a focus between the southwestern Kurpfalz and Swabian regions, where police have launched major morning raids against a biker gang.

The state Interior Ministry in Baden Württemberg has outlawed three of its chapters. Hundreds of police officers mobilized in the early hours of the morning.

The major IG Metall trade union is planning further strikes in the carmaking sector and other metalworking industries, with an announcement anticipated later in the day.

To the north, near Hanover, police report an apparent car attack injuring three men overnight.

And in the spirit of offering the public service journalism people are truly thirsting for, we'll have some info on the average and localized pricing of mulled wine or Glühwein at Christmas markets this year, as the early birds start to open their doors to visitors. (Yes, already!)

Stay tuned for updates on all this and anything else of note in or pertaining to Germany as the day progresses.

#780. Manchester City v Fulham: Premier League – live

⚽️ Premier League updates from the 12.30pm GMT kick-off ⚽️ Live scores | Table | Follow on TikTok | And email Barry

90+2 min: Cherki advances into the Fulham box and tries to create and angle for a shot. Sander Berge and Antonee Robinson combine to put a stop to his gallop.

90+1 min: Fulham lay siege to the City box and Sander Berge pulls the ball across the face of goal from the byline. There’s nobody in a red shirt suitably placed to convert.

90 min: In a sight you don’t see too often, Jeremy Doku is penalised for a foul throw deep in Fulham territory.

89 min: Sander Berge plays a long ball towards the left side of the City penalty area, where Gonzalo Garcia wins it after Ruben Dias had misjudged its flight. City manage to clear their lines regardless.

87 min: Cherki robs the ball from Palacios and charges upfield from inside his own half before yielding possession back to Fulham. I have a feeling in my bones we might get a winner before this match ends but I couldn’t say which team will score it.

85 min: Affengruber is on hand to cut out a low Fernandez cross into the Fulham penalty areas that was heading towards Haaland at the far post. The flag goes up for an offside.

84 min: Erling Haaland raises his arms in sarcastic celebration after finally getting a free-kick for a foul on him by David Affengruber. Man City substitution: Enzo Fernandez on for Bouaddi.

82 min: Following good work from Haaland and Allan, Rayan Cherki has a low shot blocked at close range by Calvin Bassey. Fulham double substitution: Tom Cairney on for Muniz and Cesar Palacios on for Sessegnon.

80 min: Manchester City substitution from three minutes ago: Allan Elias is on for Iliman Ndiaye.

79 min: Kenny Tete runs into Gvardiol as he tries to advance down the right wing and the ball goes out for a Fulham throw-in.

77 min: Both sides feel they can win this game and Fulham show their intent by bringing the Spanish striker Gonzalo Garcia on for Oscar Bobb. In the City ranks, Josko Gvardiol comes on for Nico O’Reilly.

74 min: Fulham win another corner as Khusanov swings a high boot to prevent Sessegnon from getting to a cross from the right to the far post. Shea Charles picks out Rodrigo Muniz with his inswinger but the Fulham striker is unable to steer the ball on target. Donnarumma gets booked for dissent after complaining to the referee about being blocked as he attempted to get to the ball.

72 min: Kenny Tete does superbly to stick out a leg for a well-timed tackle to prevent Jeremy Doku getting a shot on the turn away from near the penalty spot in the Fulham penalty area.

70 min: Fulham double-substitution: Hugo Larsson and Antonee Robinson come on for Josh King and Alex Iwobi. Manchester City substitution: Rayan Cherki replaces Phil Foden.

68 min: Donnarumma is forced into action again, saving a low Calvin Bassey shot from a tight angle with his legs. It’s a corner for Fulham, which Ruben Dias heads clear from Iwobi.

67 min: Oooof! Sander Berge plays Rodrigo Muniz in behind the City defence and the Fulham striker’s shot is saved by a big outstretched Donnarumma left hand.

65 min: Haaland wins the race to a weighted through ball from Bouaddi and pulls the ball inside to Anderson. Hes first touch is sublime and tees up a low shot towards the far corner. The ball trundles inches wide of the upright.

63 min: I feel I might have been a little harsh in suggesting Bernd Leno should have done better for that Anderson goal. It was right in the corner.

61 min: The mood at the Etihad is improved immeasurably and Ryan Sessegnon is lucky to avoid a booking for a hold on Ndiaye that prevented the City winger from running on to a Haaland pass.

59 min: That was an outstanding volley from Anderson, who watched the ball closely as it dropped his way from a headed clearnace. The contact couldn’t have been sweeter.

Manchester City equalise! It’s a splendid finish from Elliot Anderson, who sends a low volley through a thicket of legs and under the dive of Leno from the edge of the penalty area, when the ball was cleared his way from a corner.

56 min: Doku slips the ball to Bouaddi on the edge of the area but his shot is blocked by Affengruber, who is doing the defending of several men.

55 min: Ten minutes into the second half and City are showing no discernible signs of improvement following their abject first-half showing. It’s all far too easy for Fulham, who have not beaten City since 2009 and are trying to avoid their 21st consecutive defeat in all competitions at the hands of their hosts.

53 min: Fulham win a throw-in deep in City territory. They play it short and work the ball back to Calvin Bassey near the halfway line.

51 min: The ball breaks to Phil Foden in the Fulham penalty area but his shot is blocked out for a corner by David Affengruber, who appears to be having the game of his life. Nothing comes of the set-piece.

49 min: Fulham win a free-kick wide on the left and proceed to pen City deep inside their own half after the ball is swung into the penalty areas. City finally play the ball out despite assorted Fulham players snapping menacingly at their heels.

48 min: Give the people what they want – there’s a huge roar of approval from the stands as Haaland breaks into a sprint to press Leno as he deals with a backpass.

46 min: Phil Foden gets the ball rolling for a City side that have, somewhat surprisingly, not made any changes during the break. Almost immediately they lose the ball to Oscar Bobb, whose delivery towards the City penalty area is headed away by Nico O’Reilly.

That disallowed Haaland goal: According to Ifab Law 12 “A goalkeeper is considered to be in control of the ball with their hand(s)/arm(s) when: the ball is between their hands/arms or between their hand(s)/arm(s) and any surface (eg ground, own body.”

Going by that and having seen several more replays, it’s this humble minute-by-minute reporter’s view that the decision to disallow Haaland’s effort was the correct one.

Some correspondence: “What a strange, but entertaining half,” writes Justin Kavanagh. “Haaland looks like he couldn’t buy a goal, while David Affengruber seems to be channeling his inner Bobby Moore in a Fulham shirt.”

“Ref here,” writes Paul Pooley. “Two hands is not the standard. Control can be as little as one finger on the ball against the turf. The question is did Haaland play the ball when Leno had a hand on the ball against the ground.”

“No doubt there’ll be focus on the disallowed goal (can see why not given, even if soft),” writes Shaun T. “But I also think it should be highlighted what an awful miss/bad connection from Haaland that was too. He had time to watch that Ndiaye cross right onto his foot and should really be burying that.”

Half-time: Fulham lead courtesy of an excellent striked from Rodrigo Muniz, while City will feel they were unfairly denied an equaliser when Erling Haaland was penalised for bundling the ball over the line when Bernd Leno was in full control of it. It looked a harsh decision but the real story of this first half has revolved around how sluggish and off the pace City’s players have looked. Enzo Maresca has a big job on his hands if his side are to avoid their fourth consecutive top flight defeat.

45+2 min: The half ends with Bernd Leno saving easily from a half-hearted Jeremy Doku shot.

45+1 min: David Affengruber has been outstanding at the back for Fulham today and excels again here. He stands his ground to take the ball off Iliman Ndiaye’s toe after the City winger had jinked his way into the Fulham box and was about to unleash a shot.

44 min: With his arm in the air appealing for a free-kick that isn’t awarded, Nico O’Reilly completely switches off and allows Oscar Bobb to nip in behind him and shoot on goal from about eight yards out. Donnarumma denies the Fulham winger with an excellent save. That’s shocking – City are a mess!

41 min: Elliot Anderson advances towards the Fulham penalty area after winning the ball and plays a weighted pass to Nico O’Reilly. He eschews a shooting opportunity in favour of teeing up Haaland with a sideways pass but the Norwegian’s poor effort is way off-target. It takes a deflection to go out for a corner, from which nothing comes.

40 min: The City fans aren’t happy with their team’s extremely lacklustre performance and are jerring and whistling their players for not pressing Bernd Leno and assorted Fulham defenders as they pass the ball around the back.

37 min: City win a corner after good work from Jeremy Doku, who appeared to be fouled on the edge of the City area by Kenny Tete. From that set-piece, City win another. Phil Foden plays it short to Anderson near the edge of the penalty area but Fulham force their hosts backwards.

35 min: Erling Haaland sends a wild shot high and wide after running on to a beautifully weighted pass through the Fulham penalty area from Phil Foden.

33 min: Bernd Leno stands over the stationary ball after receiving a backpass and makes no effort to do anything with it, letting the clock tick down. Various City fans impatiently roar at Erling Haaland to press the German goalkeeper and force him into some sort of action.

32 min: A Shea Charles cross from the right aimed towards Rodrigo Muniz is headed clear. Manchester City are looking very flat and vulnerable this afternoon.

30 min: A stray pass from Affengruber to Bassey is pounced on by Iliman Ndiaye near the halway line but a promising attack breaks down when Kenny Tete wins it back in the Fulham right-back area.

28 min: I think Fulham might have got away with one there, because Leno did have two hands on the ball at one point, he didn’t appear to have it under anything resembling control as Haaland bore down on him to force it over the line with his second attempt.

24 min: Iliman Ndiaye floats a superb cross into the Fulham penalty area from the right. Haaland connects with a thigh from about three yards out. Bernd Leno stops the ball only for the City striker to force the ball over the line with his follow-up. Haaland thinks he’s scored but his “goal” is disallowed because Leno is adjudged to have had two hands on the ball. Did he? I’m not so sure.

#779. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

#778. The Chelsea loanee turning heads and Championship defenders at 17

Ryan Kavuma-McQueen joined Portsmouth on loan over the summer

Explosive pace, infectious energy on the field and bundles of footballing ability.

At just 17, Ryan Kavuma-McQueen has looked at home in the Championship since embarking on his first loan move away from Chelsea.

With one senior appearance to his name at Stamford Bridge, the winger swapped west London for the south coast in August and has quickly become a fan favourite at Fratton Park.

Indeed, Kavuma-McQueen was so impressive in a recent game against Sheffield United, Pompey boss John Mousinho admitted their tactic essentially became - pass him the ball as much as possible.

"For a 17-year-old to come in and play as many games as he has done is a real achievement," the Portsmouth head coach told BBC Sport.

"He's been brilliant to work with and has been absolutely unplayable in some games, for us it's now about getting him consistently to that level.

"It's very easy to forget that he's only 17 because of the way that he plays and how he carries himself - overall it's been an excellent loan so far and we're really excited to see how he goes for the rest of the season."

At international level, Kavuma-McQueen has played 31 matches for England's youth sides and scored 29 goals.

One of his most recent for England Under-18s was a stunning strike that saw him beat a number of defenders with some smart footwork before launching a right-footed rocket into the top corner from 25 yards.

For Portsmouth, he scored seven minutes into his first Championship start and has registered two assists, contributing to winning points for the Blues in games against Blackburn Rovers and Sheffield United.

"No other so-called 'big six' Premier League club has a fully homegrown 17-year-old on loan in the Championship," said BBC football news reporter Nizaar Kinsella.

"This is a source of pride within Chelsea's academy. At Championship level, only Preston's George Gryba and Wolves' Charlie Holt have made appearances at a younger age this season.

"It is clear that Kavuma-McQueen finds playing against opponents of his own age relatively straightforward.

"Securing a loan move was so important this summer, without European football, and with a large number of wide options available, opportunities were always likely to be limited at Chelsea."

So far this season, Kavuma-McQueen has featured predominantly on the left but has also played on the right wing of Portsmouth's attack.

He leads the Championship in some attacking metrics, completing the most successful take-ons (30) and attempting the joint-most dribbles (55) in the division.

He is also in the top 10 for drives into the box and carries ending in shots.

The Blues have a number of wide attackers to choose from, with Abu Kamara and Josh Murphy both proven at this level, but the teenager has displayed his credentials to play in their starting XI, making nine starts in the Championship with a further five appearances off the bench.

If he can remain fit then he will undoubtably be an important player for the rest of the 2026-27 campaign, but a sustained period of health is far from straightforward in a relentless league and a busy festive schedule to come.

Regardless of the impact that Kavuma-McQueen has over the rest of the season, there is no doubt that the experience he will gain from this loan should serve him well going forward.

Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho on Ryan Kavuma-McQueen

Mousinho has praised the winger's character after an injury setback in September after falling over advertising hoardings at Fratton Park.

He suffered a double fracture on his right hand, but opted against surgery and now wears a splint and cast for games which has delayed his full recovery to around eight weeks.

The Portsmouth boss admitted that he was probably not managing the injury in the most ideal way, but believed his decision to play on provided an insight into his mentality of wanting to make the most of the loan move.

"From a football perspective he's managing it unbelievably well and he hasn't shied away from anything on the pitch," Mousinho added.

"It's never been a concern of mine and the fact that he wanted to play and didn't want surgery tells us everything we need to know about the lad."

Pompey are enjoying a positive start to their third season back in the second tier having won promotion from League One in 2024.

They are 11th in the table and just two points outside of the newly expanded play-off positions.

Kavuma-McQueen has played plenty of minutes already - his 719 is comfortably the highest among Championship players 18 and under, but there is a slight concern Pompey could become victims of his success in terms of his immediate future.

"Arguably in the first part of Portsmouth's season, he was their best player," said BBC Radio Solent commentator Andrew Moon.

"He's fast, skillful and exciting to watch. He's also able to cope with a physical league that most teenagers can't.

"His output did drop off before the international break but there will always be some ups and downs with such a young player. Mousinho has been managing his minutes very carefully.

"He's already being watched by other clubs and Chelsea could recall him in January to send elsewhere. Portsmouth will argue strongly that Fratton Park is the best place for him to continue his development."

Ryan Kavuma-McQueen has been capped by England from under-15 to under-18 level

For his parent club, Kavuma-McQueen is seen as a talent with a genuine chance of making it at the club, despite fierce competition among the wide players already in the squad.

He joined the west London club at under-eight level and signed a scholarship in July 2025.

Prior to his move to the south coast he travelled with the senior Chelsea squad for their pre-season tour, starting against Western Sydney Wanderers down-under before his loan move.

Chelsea already have a host of highly-rated teenagers out on loan, including Jesse Derry (Sporting), Dastan Satpayev (Burnley), Reggie Walsh (Wigan Athletic), Shim Mheuka (Celtic) and Landon Emenalo (Celtic).

The club also lost Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool and Ryan McAidoo to Man City in 2024, which remains a sore point within the Surrey-based academy.

In an era of lucrative deals for players between top academies, Chelsea have not lost a player since but had to fight hard to keep Kavuma-McQueen before he signed his first professional contract in January.

By securing a move to the Championship, Kavuma-McQueen can continue his development at a high level, and his performances at Fratton Park have been noted by influential figures back in west London.

"We speak to them [Chelsea] all the time and that's a positive thing," Mousinho added.

"They would like Ryan to play as much as possible but also get the exposure of what it's like to be in and out of a first team and experience the highs and lows of football that has real consequence.

"That's been amazing in terms of Ryan's development and making sure that we keep on top of him physically and mentally.

"We have both clubs working really hard to make sure that happens and both clubs working really hard in conjunction with each other."

#777. NFL great Brady could buy Chelsea stake

Tom Brady is a seven-time Super Bowl champion

American football great Tom Brady is looking to invest in Chelsea through ownership group Clearlake Capital.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner has recently divested his stake in Championship club Birmingham City, which he bought into following Tom Wagner's Knighthead Capital takeover in 2023.

It now appears he could move into Chelsea, where he has a positive relationship with influential co-owner Behdad Eghbali, having been a star guest at the after-party following the club's Club World Cup triumph in 2025.

Brady would have no voting rights or control at Chelsea, although the ownership group could look to appoint him to the board if it suited all parties.

The move is not said to be linked to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter's Â£950m sale of their stakes to Clearlake Capital, which must be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss remains a significant minority stakeholder at Stamford Bridge.

The investment is also not part of a funding round, according to senior sources, and is not intended to dilute Clearlake Capital's control.

However, other interested parties are said to have approached them about investing since Boehly and Walter agreed a deal to leave.

Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Following the end of his playing career he acquired a stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.

On top of that, Brady's commitments include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

#776. On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#775. Key questions as Scottish Premiership returns

Wouter Wrancken under pressure; Mario Frick's beginning; John McGlynn the saviour

The Scottish Premiership returns with an all-action Saturday after what was a bleak international break for the national side.

Most of the intrigue is on men who will not make a pass or a tackle. There is one new manager, one who is being touted for the Scotland job, another who has turned around a failing side and one who is increasingly under pressure.

And none of those are in charge of Old Firm teams. The managerial status at Celtic and Rangers is relatively settled, but of course that can change in the space of 90 minutes.

This is your essential guide to Saturday's action.

Aberdeen have a new head coach for their basement battle with Kilmarnock, with Mario Frick replacing Stephen Robinson

The Liechtensteiner was a fine striker in his day and his main mission is to get the Dons firing in front of goal again.

Frick favoured two up top while in charge of Luzern, so he needs to find a way to supply Kevin Nisbet and Ayoub Mouloua.

Connor Ronan could hold the key to improving a sorry set of attacking statistics, but the Irish midfielder will need to show more than he has since his summer arrival.

Aberdeen have 12 goals from 12 league games. Kilmarnock have 13 from 13. Both sides have amassed just four points from their past six outings, so this may well be something of a scrap.

Killie were slightly more menacing in a 0-0 draw at Pittodrie in September and the same could be said of a League Cup quarter-final at Rugby Park a week later, although the Dons did well to prevail on penalties after a red card early in the second half.

The Ayrshire side have the league's worst defensive record by a distance, conceding three or more goals on six occasions. However, manager Neil McCann will have been heartened by a tenacious showing in the 1-0 loss at Celtic Park last time out.

With four successive matches coming against sides currently in the bottom six before taking on the Dundee duo, McCann will view this pre-Christmas sequence as vital.

Hear from Aberdeen's Mario Frick at first press conference

Of the leading sides, Celtic have the easier-looking task at home to St Mirren, who have enjoyed just one victory in their past 40 visits to the east end of Glasgow in all competitions.

However, the league leaders have not kicked on since thrashing Heart of Midlothian last month, drawing with Dundee United and losing to Falkirk either side of narrow and unconvincing wins over Hibernian and Kilmarnock.

That 1-0 win at home to Killie was just a second clean sheet in seven Premiership matches for the champions.

Celtic came from behind to win 2-1 in Paisley in September, with Yang Hyun-Jun grabbing the second. The winger's return should add dynamism to their attack.

Since pushing Celtic all the way at home, St Mirren have picked up a mere four points from nine matches.

Rangers go to Motherwell off the back of a 2-0 win away to the Buddies, extending their unbeaten league run to 10 games and maintaining the best defensive numbers in the table.

The goals came from a contentious penalty and a deflected shot and manager Derek McInnes spoke of the need to sharpen up in the final third after several promising situations broke down.

After a six-game losing slump that began in Govan, Motherwell have steadied the ship and played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with Dundee United before the break that included a combined 40 efforts on goal.

Well shared the points with Rangers at Fir Park last season, scoring late on both occasions, and, while not the force they were after so many departures, still retain a core of players who celebrated victory at Ibrox in April.

Rangers have the momentum, although recent draws away to Dundee and Hearts underline the fact they remain a work in progress under McInnes.

New manager Frick to take Aberdeen back to basics

We'll only sell if offer makes club blink - McInnes

Five wins on the spin have propelled Falkirk up to third place and they will be big favourites to extend that run at home to St Johnstone.

Celtic beaten, Hearts hammered... fans are talking about European qualification, having ended a five-year stint in League 1 in May 2024.

John McGlynn continues to work his magic on a meagre budget, with new arrivals Jacob Murrell, Owen Eames, Finley Barbrook and Deniss Melniks hitting the ground running.

Ethan Ross is lapping up a new lease of life, while older heads Scott Bain and Liam Henderson have never been better, although the loss of influential skipper Brad Spencer is a huge blow.

The Perth Saints will be no pushovers. They too are punching above their weight with just four defeats in 13 on their return to the top flight.

Rangers are the only side to beat Simo Valakari's men since a 1-1 draw with Falkirk at McDiarmid Park in mid-September.

That was the first league meeting of the clubs since 2010, but, with such astute managers in place, it looks like this can remain a top-flight rivalry for a good while yet.

Have Hibs turned a corner and have Hearts fallen down a hole?

Marink Reedijk lost his first three games after replacing David Gray, but now the Hibs head coach is looking for a third successive victory at home to Dundee United.

The Easter Road side clambered out of the bottom spot in style, thumping Aberdeen 4-0 at Pittodrie after coming from behind to stun their Edinburgh rivals in the League Cup semi-final.

Hearts went into that game at Hampden as heavy favourites and across the following seven days were outplayed by the team sitting eighth in the Swiss Super League and walloped by Falkirk, ending their 19-month long unbeaten home record in the league.

A growing injury list has hampered Hearts, but Wouter Vrancken's methods are being questioned, with only Kilmarnock conceding more goals in the league.

A visit to Dundee is next and Steven Pressley's much-improved team have only been defeated once at Dens Park so far.

United have also been a breath of fresh air, adopting a new swashbuckling style that has yielded four wins and four draws in their past nine games.

Hibs have taken significant strides, particularly in the midfield area, but this will be a real test of their progress. There were 11 goals in the two games against United at Easter Road last season and another big score would not be a surprise.
