#709. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

#708. Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more important when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

"We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish."

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source

To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different."

Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

The difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today."

Whether you just got together or you're practically married, there are gift ideas for every kind of partner.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission.

Spare a thought for the humble boyfriend. Gift-giving for significant others can be tough, and “boyfriend” can mean a lot of things, from just-got-together to long-term partner. Do you go all out on your new boo and risk overdoing it, or play it cool and risk playing it too cool? Of course, there’s the happy middle, which is where we (hopefully) come in.

Below, you’ll find carefully chosen gifts for boyfriends of all stripes. There are gifts for the cinephile boyfriend who can rattle off his Letterboxd top four at any time (this is The Hollywood Reporter, after all), the fashion-forward guy with a mile-long Mr. Porter wishlist and even gifts for the guy who promises, year after year, that he doesn’t want anything. Gifting for a big reader, but not sure what he’s into?

Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. MAVEN launched to find out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

After its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

"The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come."

MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

An investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

"Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, said of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here."

#705. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

#704. Hello Sunshine’s Lauren Neustadter Stepping Down at Year’s End (Exclusive)

The longtime president of film and television is leaving after nearly a decade at Reese Witherspoon’s company and on the heels of a recent ownership change.

Changes continue at Reese Witherspoon’s Hello Sunshine, where the company’s top creative executive, Lauren Neustadter, is stepping down at year’s end. The longtime collaborators announced the move on Friday afternoon.

“Lauren’s taste, passion and leadership have been integral to Hello Sunshine’s film and television success,” said Witherspoon, founder of Hello Sunshine. “I’m so proud of what we accomplished together and grateful for her partnership and the lasting foundation she built around telling powerful, complex female-driven stories that resonate.” Related Stories Business Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine Breaks Away From Candle Media Business From 'F1' to 'Slow Horses' to 'Call My Agent!': Mediawan Executives Take Madrid Spotlight

“Building Hello Sunshine alongside Reese and our incredible team has been the privilege of a lifetime,” added Neustadter. “I’m deeply proud of all the shows and movies we’ve made, the doors we’ve opened for new voices, and the ways we have put women in the spotlight both in front of and behind the camera. I am grateful for every moment of it, and I will always be cheering for Hello Sunshine.”

Neustadter has served as president of film and television at Hello Sunshine since she joined the company in 2017. Over her tenure, she executive produced a number of TV series, including The Morning Show, Big Little Lies, Little Fires Everywhere, The Last Thing He Told Me, Truth Be Told and Surface — also spearheading adaptations of Reese’s Book Club picks Tiny Beautiful Things and Daisy Jones & The Six. This past summer, Hello Sunshine premiered Legally Blonde prequel Elle at Prime Video and Lucky on Apple TV. Neustadter also worked on features Where the Crawdads Sing, Your Place or Mine, You’re Cordially Invited and TriStar’s upcoming adaptation of The Nightingale. She will remain with the company through the end of the year to support the transition.

Her departure comes during a period of transition for Hello Sunshine. In October, Witherspoon teamed up with Mediawan to buy the company back from Candle Media. Hello Sunshine, which Witherspoon founded with Seth Rodsky in 2016, was acquired by the Blackstone-backed company in 2021 in a deal valued at $900 million.

In partnering with the growing French media company, Hello Sunshine joins a sprawling portfolio of entertainment brands that includes Chernin Entertainment and Plan B Entertainment. But the shift has also meant changes at the company. Hello Sunshine’s sale was followed by layoffs its direct-to-consumer division.

Prior to her near-decade at Hello Sunshine, Neustadter worked at old Fox — where she was senior vice president of programming at the broadcast network, overseeing such series as The Mindy Project and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. She joined the network after a tenure at 20th Century Fox, where she worked on such films as Parental Guidance and Witherspoon vehicle This Means War. While at 20th, she was included The Hollywood Reporter’s Next Gen list — the magazine’s annual assessment of the 35 fastest rising entertainment executives under the age of 35.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports.

As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

"Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect."

In the new study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

In 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar said.

In the new study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar said.

Although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down."

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar said. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events."

The scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Charles Q. Choi is a contributing writer for Space.com and Live Science. He covers all things human origins and astronomy as well as physics, animals and general science topics. #702. ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Meghie Rodrigues is a science and climate journalist in Paraná, Brazil.

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan

To err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” says Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

For the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

In the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise showed a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them quickly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is important; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn important lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

Back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

Then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

She kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a new professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a new species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a big deal for our laboratory in 20164.

In 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a big genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

In my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

Two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

When I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s big phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the new species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more new things.

Now I realize how important it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley says that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

In the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, showed me a new way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

In well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a big gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

But the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

#701. Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans

A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

#700. Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

Materials provided by University of Missouri-Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#699. TV Ratings: CMA Awards Score Seven-Year High

The show delivers its biggest audience of the 2020s so far.

The 60th CMA Awards delivered their largest TV audience of the decade.

The Nov. 18 awards averaged 7.62 million viewers on ABC and Disney+, the best same-day total for the awards since 2019 (when it brought in more than 11 million viewers). Wednesday’s show finished just ahead of the 7.57 million viewers for the 2022 awards — with the caveat that Nielsen has made several changes to the way it measures ratings in the years since then.

The CMA Awards drew a 1.01 rating among adults 18-49 (equivalent to about 1.37 million people in the demographic), the first time the show has cleared a 1.0 rating since 2022. The telecast grew by 26 percent in viewers and 55 percent in adults 18-49 from a year ago (6.04 million viewers, 0.65 rating in the 18-49 demo). Related Stories TV Streaming Ratings: Rough Week for Original Series, 'From' Remains No. 1 Overall Music Taylor Swift Performs "Our Song" and "I Knew It, I Knew You" at the CMAs

Ella Langley set a record with six wins at the awards, including entertainer of the year. Her long-running No. 1 hit “Choosin’ Texas” won CMA Awards for song, single and music video of the year.

Along with Langley’s big night, the CMA Awards featured a performance by Taylor Swift — her first at the ceremony since 2013 — and a tribute to Dolly Parton that featured Vince Gill and host Lainey Wilson performing a duet of “I Will Always Love You.” Several other artists paid tribute to Parton during the show and on the red carpet beforehand.

ABC’s annual Countdown to the CMAs special on Tuesday also earned multi-year ratings highs. Hosted by Robin Roberts, the show drew just under 3 million viewers, its best showing since 2023.

#697. A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections."

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon."

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids."

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful."

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come."

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.
